abstract: I have been associated with the telegraph service for 40 years. During the first ten years I saw little progress. We looked askance at the power engineer; he was not to be relied upon, and so, rather than take unnecessary risks, we depended on primary cells to supply whatever voltages we required. articleTitle: The Lure of Rhodesia. Modern-day travel to the world's wonder sights
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The remarkable development which the last few decades have witnessed in the Union and beyond its borders has brought about a keener and more widespread desire, amongst a growing population, for the pleasures of travel. While the popularity of a trip overseas still induces many to undertake a long voyage, there is an increasing number of South Africans for whom the great country in which they live holds unending fascination. The numerous overland safaris and excursion parties which depart from the Union northward bound, and, moreover, rail-travel groups, indicate that “wanderlust” is definitely abroad in the once “dark continent.” A few hardy spirits who have the leisure and are indifferent to the strain and even hardship of the road have set themselves the life long task of knowing Africa at first hand, and a few of these have achieved this alluring goal, but for the vast majority the ease and comfort afforded by train-travel on the South African and Rhodesian Railways is by far the more preferable, and the effortless journey is richer in pleasurable experience.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Photography of lightning strokes with the Boys camera has shown that each separate stroke is of a dual nature, consisting of a leader and a return portion. It has been shown that the return stroke travels from ground to cloud, passing outwards along the brandies when it reaches branching points of the leader. The charge on the leader branches passes in this manner to ground. It has also been shown that there is a marked diminution in the intensity of light emitted from the main channel after the return stroke has passed a prominent branch.

The speed of propagation of a surge through the end windings of an alternator is about 600 feet per microsecond, while in the slots it is only one-tenth of this value. Knowing the length of one turn of the winding, the time for a surge to traverse one turn can be calculated, and when taken in conjunction with the rate of rise of voltage will give the voltage between turns, the maximum value so obtained being on the end turns.

articleTitle: The technical development of the telegraph service in the union of South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The telegraph system of the Union of South Africa dates back to the comparatively early days of the old Cape Colony and the other provinces which now form the Union. There are still many routes standing to-day which were built by the pioneers of the system long before there were any defined roads, and consequently were constructed straight across country from point to point. They were built with iron poles, and carried usually only one or two galavnised iron wires of either No. 8 or No. 6 gauge. Some of these wires are still up after 50 and more years, as such wire on the high veld has an extraordinarily long life. These old circuits were worked on the morse system, and the received signals were received on an “inker” or read by ear from a sounder. Belaying systems were not then developed, so that the high resistance of the circuits necessitated retransmission from point to point by hand sending. Up to the time of the Anglo-Boer War, development lay chiefly in increasing the number of routes throughout the country and in establishing fairly large “retransmitting” offices, such as. Fort Beaufort and Kingwilliamstown, to mention only- two well-known offices. At the. time of the Anglo-Boer War, several improvements were, introduced, such as repeater stations; which enabled direct working to be introduced over very long distances, and the Wheatstone automatic system. This system was the first method of obtaining a greater output of traffic over a line than was possible by hand sending. With this system, messages are run through a transmitter at speed corresponding to about 100 words per minute At the receiving end of the line a sensitive inker of Wheatstone's design printed the message in dots and dashes, which was then read and transcribed on to a message-form. This system, which is still in use for emergency working, held the field for all long and busy circuits up to 1913. At this time the inventions of F. G. Creed were introduced to improve working between Capetown and Johannesburg. This system was a development of the Wheatstone system with the following modifications: The transmitting tape was prepared by means of a keyboard perforator. The transmitter was substantially the same as Wheatstone's, but at the receiving end a mechanical reperforator was used, which, operated by the received signals, produced a punched tape exactly similar to the tape in the transmitter. This tape has a twofold use. It can be used to send the messages on it to another station, or it can be run through a printer, which mechanically converts the morse signals into Roman characters and prints them on a tape which is gummed to the message form. This system gave excellent service for many years, and is, in fact, still doing so. The speed of working is usually limited to about 80 words per minute. It can operate faster, but this is found to be the highest economical speed. It will be appreciated that the Creed-Morse system is actually a development from the earlier morse systems. Fig. 1 shows the perforated tape used for sending in this system and the corresponding characters, from which it will be seen that the actual signals sent to line are the ordinary morse signals, in which the various characters differ widely in length. The received perforated tape is exactly the same as the tape prepared for transmission, and it is passed through the printer, which, by means of a series of selecting rods which pass through the perforations in the tape, set up various combinations on a series of 20 combs, permitting the selection of some 50 characters on a type wheel. The machine on exhibition will demonstrate the system of printing, and I am sure you will appreciate the genius of its designer when the variations in lengths of the various characters on the perforated tape are examined.

articleTitle: “The propagation of radiated waves from various antennae systems, and the effect of earth conductivity thereon” (under the direction of Mr. Hilarius of the African Broadcasting Co., Ltd.)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Despite the vast strides which have been made in the development of radio communication and apparatus, there is one factor, namely, the antennae systems, which has not shared in this rapid progress until lately. The reason is not far to seek or difficult to appreciate when the difficulties associated with theoretical work on this subject are considered. There are many factors which influence the radiation from antennae and whose effects cannot be accurately computed, one of the chief being the effect of the earth. It is well known that a wave propagated along the earth is attenuated, but the extent to which this attenuation occurs depends so much on the nature of the ground that an accurate calculation becomes extremely difficult. The early investigators were aware of this attenuation and attempted to embody in their formulae for the field strength set up by antennae, a factor which would take into account the loss due to attenuation, but it became evident that the phenomenon was too complicated to be accounted for by a single factor.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The President: Under the heading of “General Business,” I would like to mention that we have several visitors with us to-night. I would particularly mention Mr. F. K. Webber, President of the Associated Scientific and Technical Societies; Mr. Martin Epton, Honorary Treasurer of the Associated Societies; Dr. E. J. Hamlin, President of the South African Institution of Engineers; Mr. E. C. Ranson, President of the Chemical, Metallurgical and Mining Society of South Africa; Mr. W. H. Tredre, President of the Association of Certificated (S.A.) Mechanical and Electrical Engineers, and Mr. H. R. Raikes, Principal of the University of the Witwatersrand. We are very pleased indeed to see these gentlemen with us to-night, and we hope they will have an interesting time. They cannot, however, come here without having to do something; so I will first call on Mr. Webber to say a few words.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Born in Cambridgeshire, England, in 1874, Mr. Clayden received his early training at Faraday House. After holding the positions of Borough Electrical Engineer to the Corporations of Morley and Middlesbrough (England), he came to South Africa in 1802, and was appointed Resident Mechanical and Electrical Engineer to the Consolidated Main Reef Mines and Estate, which position he held until 1914. In February of that year he joined the General Mining and Finance Corporation as Consulting Electrical Engineer, and became Consulting Mechanical and Electrical Engineer to the group in September, 1919, which position he held until his death.

abstract: Mr. Campbell was the second sun of the Rev. and Mrs. A. H. Campbell, of Brassington, England, and he was educated at St. Leonard's and Malvern College. After serving a pupilage with the civil and mechanical engineering firm of Messrs. Thornewill & Warham, Burton - on - Trent, he gained experience in the design, manufacture and erection of mining machinery with various firms in England. He also gamed experience on the Continent, particularly in France, and came to South Africa in 1895.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The President: The next item on the agenda forms the last duty I have to perform as your President; it is a very pleasing one, namely, the induction of the incoming President. It is usual to congratulate the new President, but I am not going to follow the usual course; I am going to congratulate the Institute on being so fortunate as having such a suitable person as Mr. Joseph White as its President. (Loud Applause.) And I am going to congratulate myself and the other Past Presidents on being able to rest assured that the interests of the Institute, which we all have at heart are placed in such able hands. (Hear, hear.) Mr. White is well known to you all, and I need say no more. Mr. White, I now have pleasure in vacating the chair in your favour; and I feel that you will receive the same support from your Vice-Presidents and Members of Council as I did, and I wish you a pleasant and successful year of office. (Applause.)
